newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro-bourses fall but avoid Wall St selloff.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro-bourses fall but avoid Wall St selloff.

text.p: Interest rate fears called the tune on European financial markets on Friday, sending the dollar rising but wiping billions of dollars off share markets.
A 160 point plunge in the Dow Jones Industrials Average overnight hammered investor sentiment in Europe and stock markets across the continent opened with sharp falls.
The dollar, in contrast benefited from rekindled speculation about a rise in U.S. interest rates and moved moderately higher before slipping back from its peaks during the morning.
After the initial stocks reaction, some share values also began to creep back up and some analysts questioned fears of a major bloodletting.
Dealers in London, Europe's biggest stock market, said activity was likely to be subdued ahead of the weekend and U.S. economic data scheduled for later in the day was also likely to cap losses.
"I don't think it will be as exciting as some people believe," said one trader. "I see us wobbling a bit, but the wheels won't be coming off."
A raft of U.S. economic data was due to be released at 1330 GMT, including producer price figures and industrial production figures for February.

Thursday's retail sales and weekly jobless claims data sparked the Dow's fifth steepest fall in point terms by underlining a growing likelihood that the Federal Reserve will act to head off inflationary pressures by tightening rates after its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on March 25.
New York analysts cited a stiff bond market sell-off as the primary catalyst for the decline in stocks.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury fell nearly a full point to drive the yield up to 6.96 percent, its highest level in nearly six months.
That was reflected in Europe where British government gilts fell 7/32 at the open and German bund futures posted early losses too.
Among Europe's big three bourses, Paris suffered the worst, the CAC-40 index posting a decline of 1.5 percent by 1000 GMT although it was off its early lows.

Paris traders said the bourse was partly sustained by expectations that higher U.S. rates would push up the dollar and one broker said the selling pressure was limited. "We've been falling for three days now," he said, adding that there appeared to be strong support at 2,595 points. "That seems to be holding."

Shares in Assurances Generales de France fell 4.57 percent to 204.70 francs, the biggest fall in the CAC index, after the group expressed interest in bidding for state insurer GAN, which is slated for privatisation.
The German market, which was the worst performer of the big three on Thursday, followed the trend but only fell modestly.
Dealers said the German market was drawing some support from the renewed strength of the dollar.
The DAX-30 index of leading shares was down 17.78 points at 1000 GMT at 3,332.03.
The continued strength of Deutsche Telekom, up 10 pfennigs at 36.75 marks in decent volumes, also lent support.
London shares cut the worst of their losses by mid-morning, but the FTSE index was still down half a percentage point at 4,375.
Despite turmoil across the Atlantic some traders said London might prefer to remain focused on domestic events for the time being.
"People have spent a lot of effort getting cash into this market for the last two or three weeks and I'm not sure they are ready to take it all out again," said one equities salesman.

Among early share movers, B.A.T. Industries Plc took centre stage, losing as much as 33p to 520 before recovering to 535.5 following a Mississippi court ruling which sent U.S. tobacco stocks tumbling.
Although the dollar made immediate gains after Thursday's U.S. data, it edged back during the European morning from its highs of 1.7100 marks and 123.85 yen.

"The retail sales report was yet another catalyst to point out to people that the same fundamental dollar-bull story is as valid now as it was a month ago," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS in London.
CURRENCIES AT 1020 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.7048 marks and 123.58 yen, compared Thursday's late European levels of 1.7030 marks and 122.92 yen.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1000 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 22.0 points, or 0.5 percent, at 4,375.7.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was 39.42 points, or 1.5 percent, at 2,736.71.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was down 17.78 points, or 0.53 percent, at 3,332.03.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was quoted unchanged at $353.05. Silver was quoted two cents higher at $5.30. --
